title: AI office work: write a brief that produces reviewable files
description: Specify business outcomes, authoritative context, correction rules, and artifact acceptance for everyday AI tasks.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: OfficeDex: Vibe Officing: AI for Everyday Office Work

coverAlt: AI office work: write a brief that produces reviewable files: Audience brief, Source context, Artifact constraints, Correction loop.
intro: A useful AI office brief states the audience, business outcome, deliverables, authoritative sources, and acceptance checks. It should also say what must remain unresolved when evidence is missing. Review the generated files and correct factual rules across every artifact before authorizing distribution.

sections.title: Specify the result and source authority
sections.html:
State who will use the artifact and what decision or action it supports. A request to create a report is incomplete without audience, purpose, scope, and output format. Add required sections, length, tone, and any fixed template or brand requirements. Specify which facts must come from supplied sources and which points should remain open if evidence is missing. Keep technical implementation choices out of the brief unless they affect the result. The authoring tool may choose its own process, but it should not have to guess the business outcome or the standard by which the artifact will be reviewed.

Provide the relevant materials and identify which are current, approved, historical, or tentative. If two sources disagree, name the owner who resolves the conflict or instruct the tool to flag it. Do not bury the essential source among dozens of unrelated attachments. For a numerical task, include units, period, currency, and definitions. For a policy task, distinguish existing policy from proposed changes. These labels reduce the chance that plausible but outdated information enters the output. Use approved data handling arrangements and avoid including sensitive information that the task does not require.

sections.title: Work through a monthly team pack
sections.html:
Imagine a team lead requesting a monthly pack from a staffing workbook and project notes. The brief asks for a one page summary, a staffing table, and four slides for the leadership meeting. It specifies the reporting month, excludes tentative hires from headcount, and requires unresolved project risks to remain visible. After the first draft, the lead notices that a delayed project is described as complete. The correction should point to the source, explain the status rule, and request checks across all three artifacts. Merely asking for better wording would leave the underlying factual problem unresolved.

outcome: leadership understands staffing and project risks
deliverables: one-page summary, staffing table, four slides
period: the nominated reporting month
headcount_rule: exclude tentative hires
source_rule: approved workbook governs numeric totals
review: inspect files and unresolved risks before sending

This is a business brief, not a prescribed implementation stack. Add the actual source versions and the owner who can resolve disputed status. The tool can choose an appropriate drafting process while the reviewer retains a concrete standard for the result.

When the delayed project is described as complete, correct the status rule as well as the sentence. Ask for the summary, table, slide title, and chart annotation to be checked against the same source. Otherwise a local wording repair can leave contradictory artifacts in the pack.

Keep a correction log with the requirement, source evidence, affected artifacts, and verified outcome. Reuse the improved brief next month, but update period and inputs deliberately. A reusable task card should not fossilize last month's assumptions. If the intended audience changes from internal leaders to a customer, reassess confidentiality, terminology, and approval requirements before rerunning it.

sections.title: Review outputs, not confident narration
sections.html: Open every generated file and inspect the parts that matter to the task. Verify totals, source references, tables, page layout, chart labels, and slide structure. Ask whether an ordinary colleague can edit and use the result in the intended application. Record corrections by requirement so the brief improves for the next run. Keep approval and distribution separate from drafting; a tool producing a polished artifact does not establish business authorization to send it. If the tool reports completion while a file is missing or unusable, treat the observable artifact as the authority and repair the workflow.

sections.title: Reusable task card Decision notes
sections.html:
• Describe audience, decision, deliverables, and required format.
  • Identify authoritative sources, periods, units, and unresolved conflicts.
  • State constraints and facts the tool must not invent.
  • Correct errors with evidence and check every affected artifact.
  • Inspect files and record a human approval before distribution.
